content.overview: BNS s. 27 — Act done in good faith for benefit of child or person of unsound mind, by, or by consent of guardian.
content.study:
Introduction and meaning
Act done in good faith for benefit of child or person of unsound mind, by, or by consent of guardian. BNS restatement of IPC 89. Elements are substantially the same; cite the BNS number for offences on or after 1 July 2024. BNS restatement of IPC 89. Cite the BNS number for facts on or after 1 July 2024.
In student language: BNS s. 27 is the rule on “Act done in good faith for benefit of child or person of unsound mind, by, or by consent of guardian”. The section provides that nothing which is done in good faith for the benefit of a person under twelve years of age, or person of unsound mind, by, or by consent, either express or implied, of the guardian or other person having lawful charge of that person, is an offence by reason of any harm which it may cause, or be intended by the doer to cause or be known by the doer to be likely to cause to that person:. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 27 exists so that “Act done in good faith for benefit of child or person of unsound mind, by, or by consent of guardian” has a closed legal test in Chapter III — General Exceptions. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.
Chapter setting: When an act is not an offence: mistake, accident, infancy, unsoundness, consent, compulsion — and the right of private defence.

The provision in detail
27. Nothing which is done in good faith for the benefit of a person under twelve years of age, or person of unsound mind, by, or by consent, either express or implied, of the guardian or other person having lawful charge of that person, is an offence by reason of any harm which it may cause, or be intended by the doer to cause or be known by the doer to be likely to cause to that person:

(a) the intentional causing of death, or to the attempting to cause death;

(b) the doing of anything which the person doing it knows to be likely to cause death, for any purpose other than the preventing of death or grievous hurt, or the curing of any grievous disease or infirmity;

(c) the voluntary causing of grievous hurt, or to the attempting to cause grievous hurt, unless it be for the purpose of preventing death or grievous hurt, or the curing of any grievous disease or infirmity;

(d) the abetment of any offence, to the committing of which offence it would not extend

Essential ingredients
1. Nothing which is done in good faith for the benefit of a person under twelve years of age, or person of unsound mind, by, or by consent, either express or implied, of the guardian or other person having lawful charge of that person, is an offence by reason of any harm which it may cause, or be intended by the doer to cause or be known by the doer to be likely to cause to that person:
2. (a) the intentional causing of death, or to the attempting to cause death;
3. (b) the doing of anything which the person doing it knows to be likely to cause death, for any purpose other than the preventing of death or grievous hurt, or the curing of any grievous disease or infirmity;
4. (c) the voluntary causing of grievous hurt, or to the attempting to cause grievous hurt, unless it be for the purpose of preventing death or grievous hurt, or the curing of any grievous disease or infirmity;
5. (d) the abetment of any offence, to the committing of which offence it would not extend

Statutory illustrations
Illustration (a). A, in good faith, for his child’s benefit without his child’s consent, has his child cut for the stone by a surgeon knowing it to be likely that the operation will cause the child’s death, but not intending to cause the child’s death. A is within the exception, in as much as his object was the cure of the child

Exam use: quote illustration (a), then write which ingredient of BNS s. 27 it proves. Copying the illustration without that mapping sentence does not score.

Exceptions, limitations and provisos
Provided that this exception shall not extend to––

learningObjectives: Explain parental and guardian consent for medical/beneficial acts under BNS s. 27.
Examine the four mandatory statutory provisos restricting guardian consent.
Understand the limitation regarding intentional causing of death or grievous hurt.
enhancement.definition: BNS s. 27 provides that nothing which is done in good faith for the benefit of a person under twelve years of age, or of unsound mind, by or by consent, either express or implied, of the guardian or other person having lawful charge of that person, is an offence by reason of any harm which it may cause, or be intended by the doer to cause, or be known by the doer to be likely to cause to that person.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: A guardian or person having lawful charge of a child under twelve or a person of unsound mind may lawfully consent to beneficial harm on their behalf, subject to four strict provisos safeguarding life and limb.
statutoryFramework: Chapter III — General Exceptions, BNS s. 27 (corresponding to IPC s. 89).
Beneficiary: Person under twelve years of age, or person of unsound mind.
Consent giver: Guardian or person having lawful charge.
Proviso 1: Does NOT extend to intentional causing of death or attempt to cause death.
Proviso 2: Does NOT extend to doing what doer knows likely to cause death, unless for preventing death/grievous hurt or curing grievous disease/infirmity.
Proviso 3: Does NOT extend to intentional grievous hurt or attempt, unless for preventing death/grievous hurt or curing disease.
Proviso 4: Does NOT extend to abetment of any offence to the committing of which it would not extend.
essentialIngredients: The act is done for the benefit of a child under 12 or an unsound mind person.
The act is done in good faith by or with the consent of the lawful guardian.
The act complies with all four statutory provisos.
The benefit intended is not mere pecuniary benefit.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Children under twelve and persons of unsound mind cannot give legally valid consent under s. 28. Section 27 bridges this incapacity by empowering lawful guardians to consent to necessary medical procedures or painful interventions on their behalf. However, to prevent abuse, the section attaches four non-negotiable provisos: a guardian cannot consent to the intentional killing of a child, nor to acts known to be likely to cause death or grievous hurt unless strictly necessary to cure a grievous disease or prevent death.
examples: Teaching example (Guardian consenting to surgery): A father consents to an emergency operation on his eight-year-old child to amputate a gangrenous leg. The surgeon acts in good faith. Even though grievous hurt is caused, Proviso 3 permits it to cure a grievous disease. Section 27 protects both father and doctor.

Teaching example (Cruel punishment): A school guardian severely burns a child's hand with a heated iron as 'discipline' to cure habitual stealing. This violates Proviso 3 (intentional grievous hurt without medical justification); s. 27 is unavailable.
distinctions: Section 26 vs Section 27: Section 26 requires consent from the victim himself (adult of sound mind); Section 27 provides for substituted consent by a lawful guardian for a child under twelve or person of unsound mind.
Lawful chastisement vs Grievous harm: Mild parental correction may fall under de minimis (s. 33), but severe physical harm is barred by s. 27 provisos.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether a guardian who authorized an experimental chemotherapy treatment resulting in the death of a nine-year-old child is liable for homicide.
Rule: BNS s. 27 protects acts done with guardian consent for child's benefit, provided Proviso 2 is met (preventing death/grievous disease).
Application: Verify that the treatment was intended to arrest terminal leukemia, that the guardian acted in good faith, and that there was no intentional killing.
Conclusion: The act falls within s. 27 and is protected.
